dailyRead.headline: Hot PPI pressures and Iran tensions lift risk, but earnings catalysts and AI names skew rotation
dailyRead.body: Inflation momentum remains the dominant drag, with upstream prices signaling persistence that could keep yields elevated and raise the bar for risk-taking. Iran-related energy dynamics keep Brent above key levels, supporting energy names while pressuring growth equities. Earnings signals from AI-driven software, semis, and consumer tech hint at bifurcated outcomes; mega-cap platforms and AI accelerants may lead, while traditional cyclicals face patchy demand. The regime call remains cautious exposure to high-beta names until clearer macro and earnings clarity emerges; long-duration and defensives with earnings durability look preferable into week’s end. A broad macro backdrop anchored by BEA GDP second estimate and PCE context next week would be decisive for rate-path risk and equity rhythm.

cards.title: Inflation Monitor: Pipeline Pressures Grow
cards.thesis: Upstream price pressures widening beyond oil-linked channels suggest broader, persistent inflation risk that could constrain real yields and keep rate policy tighter for longer.
cards.whyItMatters: If upstream costs bleed into consumer prices, the expected inflation deceleration may falter, impacting fixed income risk premia and the pricing of long-duration assets.
cards.marketReadThrough: Bond traders may reprice curve steepening as core inflation risk remains elevated; cyclicals tied to commodity inputs could outperform if energy demand remains robust, but consumer demand could slow on higher prices.
cards.variantAngle: Differentiated inflation signal from upstream producer prices expanding independently of oil to gauge central bank policy risk and real rate trajectory.

cards.title: Stock market outlook midyear 2026 | Fidelity
cards.thesis: Oil price pressure from the Iran conflict could act as a headwind to equities even within a bull market, suggesting a bifurcated risk environment where energy-sensitive equities underperform relative to non-energy cyclicals.
cards.whyItMatters: Energy prices remain a primary volatility driver; mixed reactions within equity beta could widen, offering hedging or pair-trade opportunities between energy names and defensives.
cards.marketReadThrough: Equity beta to energy prices may diverge; portfolio tilts toward sectors with lower energy intensity could outperform if oil stays structurally firm.
cards.variantAngle: Isolated geopolitical shock channel as a differentiator rather than broad macro narrative; tests resilience of earnings in energy-sensitive sectors.

cards.title: Trump gives blasé response to rate hike possibility - Axios
cards.thesis: Policy ambiguity around rate hikes amidst a potential political event cycle could sustain volatility in rates markets, with imminent decisions likely to keep the curve anchored in a tight range.
cards.whyItMatters: Policy clarity matters for duration risk; even rhetoric without immediate action can compress or steepen curves depending on market perception of risk and credibility.
cards.marketReadThrough: Short-to-medium duration assets may trade within a narrow corridor; breakevens could grind higher if inflation signals reassert themselves, while longer-dated Treasuries remain sensitive to risk sentiment.
cards.variantAngle: Policy communication signal as a market mover, separate from actual rate moves; gauges market read on credibility and political risk timing.

professionalDrivers.title: Inflation Monitor: Pipeline Pressures Grow
professionalDrivers.summary: Upstream producer prices are surging, even in some areas not directly affected by oil prices, raising concerns of broader inflation in consumer prices.
professionalDrivers.excerpt: Inflation Monitor: Pipeline Pressures Grow | Charles Schwab Search Learn Markets and Economy Inflation Monitor: Pipeline Pressures Grow Upstream producer prices are surging, even in some areas not directly affected by oil prices, raising concerns that those cost increases could be passed on to consumers. May 26, 2026 Inflationary pressures are growing at every stage of the U.S. supply chain, and oil prices aren't entirely to blame. Consider the "core core" Producer Price Index (PPI), which tracks prices of "final demand" products and services excluding food, energy, and trade services. "Final demand" means one level up from consumer prices, and those prices rose 4.4% year over year in April. That was the biggest jump in three years. Outside the COVID-era inflation spike, it would have been the biggest increase since at least 2013. But it wasn't the only notable PPI number in the latest release. Several key PPI indexes rose at the fastest pace in three or four years. The headline final demand index jumped 6.0% year over year, while final-demand goods climbed 7.4%, driven primarily by energy . So, with Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) data for April due out Thursday, Federal Reserve policymakers will likely be watching warily for signs that price gains at the producer level are being passed on to consumers. Data source: Bureau of Labor Statistics Pressure is also building further up the supply chain. As the chart below illustrates, prices at all four stages of production for intermediate demand, which are numbered according to how close they are to final demand, rose at the fastest annual pace in at least three years in April. professionalDrivers.excerpt: Weekly Trader's Stock Market Outlook | Charles Schwab Search Learn Trading Weekly Trader's Outlook Dip Buyers Step in Midweek, Helped by Peace-Deal Hopes The S&P 500 Equal Weight and Dow Jones Industrial Average are both hitting fresh all-time highs today as investors appear optimistic about Iran negotiations ahead of the three-day weekend. May 22, 2026 • Nathan Peterson • Jim Ferraioli The Week That Was If you read last week's blog, you might recall that I had a "Moderately Bearish" forecast for this week, citing spiking Treasury yields, some technical deterioration along with a potential "sell on the news" reaction to Nvidia's earnings report. At the time of this writing, the S&P 500 index is on track to be up about 1% on the week, the Nasdaq 0.7%, and the Russell 2000 up 2.7%, so my forecast turned out to be wrong. Stocks sold off for the first two days of this week, but subsequently bounced, buoyed by easing oil prices and longer-term Treasury yields. It seems that these are the levers currently driving the near-term price action—higher oil prices seem to lift longer-Treasury yields (due to potential inflation impact), which generally triggers selling in stocks. When oil prices decline the opposite generally occurs. Of course, any development or social media post by President Donald Trump regarding the Iran conflict influences oil prices. Trump delivered a couple of posts around progress with Iran peace talks this week, but there still appears to be some sticking points preventing an actual resolution, namely Iran's nuclear enrichment and "tolling system" on the Strait of Hormuz. articles.title: Inflation Monitor: Pipeline Pressures Grow
articles.summary: Upstream producer prices are surging, even in some areas not directly affected by oil prices, raising concerns of broader inflation in consumer prices.
articles.excerpt: Inflation Monitor: Pipeline Pressures Grow | Charles Schwab Search Learn Markets and Economy Inflation Monitor: Pipeline Pressures Grow Upstream producer prices are surging, even in some areas not directly affected by oil prices, raising concerns that those cost increases could be passed on to consumers. May 26, 2026 Inflationary pressures are growing at every stage of the U.S. supply chain, and oil prices aren't entirely to blame. Consider the "core core" Producer Price Index (PPI), which tracks prices of "final demand" products and services excluding food, energy, and trade services. "Final demand" means one level up from consumer prices, and those prices rose 4.4% year over year in April. That was the biggest jump in three years. Outside the COVID-era inflation spike, it would have been the biggest increase since at least 2013. But it wasn't the only notable PPI number in the latest release. Several key PPI indexes rose at the fastest pace in three or four years. The headline final demand index jumped 6.0% year over year, while final-demand goods climbed 7.4%, driven primarily by energy . So, with Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) data for April due out Thursday, Federal Reserve policymakers will likely be watching warily for signs that price gains at the producer level are being passed on to consumers. Data source: Bureau of Labor Statistics Pressure is also building further up the supply chain. As the chart below illustrates, prices at all four stages of production for intermediate demand, which are numbered according to how close they are to final demand, rose at the fastest annual pace in at least three years in April. articles.excerpt: Weekly Trader's Stock Market Outlook | Charles Schwab Search Learn Trading Weekly Trader's Outlook Dip Buyers Step in Midweek, Helped by Peace-Deal Hopes The S&P 500 Equal Weight and Dow Jones Industrial Average are both hitting fresh all-time highs today as investors appear optimistic about Iran negotiations ahead of the three-day weekend. May 22, 2026 • Nathan Peterson • Jim Ferraioli The Week That Was If you read last week's blog, you might recall that I had a "Moderately Bearish" forecast for this week, citing spiking Treasury yields, some technical deterioration along with a potential "sell on the news" reaction to Nvidia's earnings report. At the time of this writing, the S&P 500 index is on track to be up about 1% on the week, the Nasdaq 0.7%, and the Russell 2000 up 2.7%, so my forecast turned out to be wrong. Stocks sold off for the first two days of this week, but subsequently bounced, buoyed by easing oil prices and longer-term Treasury yields. It seems that these are the levers currently driving the near-term price action—higher oil prices seem to lift longer-Treasury yields (due to potential inflation impact), which generally triggers selling in stocks. When oil prices decline the opposite generally occurs. Of course, any development or social media post by President Donald Trump regarding the Iran conflict influences oil prices. Trump delivered a couple of posts around progress with Iran peace talks this week, but there still appears to be some sticking points preventing an actual resolution, namely Iran's nuclear enrichment and "tolling system" on the Strait of Hormuz. articles.summary: Stocks could continue their historic bull market run, but higher oil prices sparked by the Iran conflict could weigh on markets.
articles.excerpt: Stock market outlook midyear 2026 | Fidelity May 20, 2026 5 min Save Close Popover Great, you have saved this article to you My Learn Profile page. Share Close Popover What's next for stocks: AI melt-up or oil crunch? Clicking a link will open a new window. Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Print Feedback --> Key takeaways Soaring earnings and AI spending are fueling a bull market with signs of resilience. An extended oil crunch could lead to higher rates and inflation that might weigh on stocks. Investors may be underestimating the severity of global energy supply stress. The path of oil prices could determine whether stocks soar or stumble. Despite a Mideast conflict that has severely disrupted global energy supplies, stocks this year have done more than climb a wall of worry; they’ve vaulted to record highs. Here’s what to keep in focus for the rest of 2026. 2026 midyear stock market outlook With the second half approaching, the stock market bull run remains largely intact. If investors continue to look past the Iran conflict and focus on earnings growth, the market could potentially ride the artificial intelligence boom’s tail to new highs. On the other hand, investors could at any time shift their focus from rising profits to the ongoing energy shock and how it may be beginning to create an inflation problem. As recent days have shown, that kind of shift in sentiment could send interest rates higher and push bond prices lower, putting pressure on stocks. Why stocks might continue their bullish run If bubbles are defined by excessive market valuations and a lack of earnings growth, we haven’t seen either so far.
